newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean coal miners clash with police, 10 injured.
newsitem.headline: Chilean coal miners clash with police, 10 injured.

text.p: Hundreds of unemployed coal miners clashed with police outside Chile's presidential palace on Monday in a furious street protest in which 10 people were injured and 28 arrested, police said.

The miners, thrown out of work last month when the government closed the state-owned Lota mine because it was unprofitable, attacked police with rocks and slingshots and stoned the headquarters of President Eduardo Frei's Christian Democratic party.
Police answered with volleys of tear gas and blasted the miners with mobile water cannons, arresting at least 28 miners, police said.

Ten people were injured, including two people who had tear gas canisters explode in their faces and a local television cameraman pelted in the head with a rock in the protests outside the Moneda presidential palace.

State coal company Enacar closed the century-old Lota pit in southern Chile last month after it had been losing money for years. The mine, 342 miles (550 km) south of Santiago, become a symbol of resistance by trade unions and the Communist Party to the country's free-market economic policies.

Wearing their hardhats and overalls and waving Chilean flags, the miners arrived en masse in Santiago on Sunday night vowing to protest outside the palace despite police warnings to crack down on any marches. Frei called the march "a provocation."

The coal miners' protest added to a spate of labour conflicts in Chile's large mining sector. Striking copper miners from the Canadian-owned Quebrada Blanca pit demonstrated in the northern city of Iquique on Monday while Frei was visiting with his Cabinet, union officials said.

The mine, owned by Vancouver-based Cominco Ltd, has been on strike since Wednesday, and about 350 workers at a much larger mine, Australian-owned Escondida, ended a two-week walkout on Friday after accepting a management wage package.
